note: Smoothed, hand-curated approximations of how fast each stream added new words to English in each half-century (each value covers the 50 years starting at its bin year). Units are a relative index, roughly proportional to new words per year, scaled so that 100 is about the rate of French borrowing at its 14th-century peak. The shapes follow published surveys of first attestations in the Oxford English Dictionary — especially the curves in Philip Durkin's Borrowed Words: A History of Loanwords in English (2014) — and standard histories of English, but they are not counts from any dataset. ‘native’ is the inherited Germanic word-stock, spread over the centuries when it was carried in and first written down; ‘english’ is new words formed inside English (compounds, derivatives, blends, coinages). Words reach the record later than speech (many Norse loans are first written down after 1150), and well-documented periods such as the age of print are over-represented, so read this as the relative shape of the river, not exact numbers.
